questions.q: Why did LLM-as-judge evaluation become the default for fast iteration, compared to human evaluation?
options: Because LLM judges are always more accurate than any human annotator
Because an LLM judge call takes seconds and costs a fraction of a cent compared to a human annotation, making it practical to re-run evaluation constantly across checkpoints and prompt variants
Because human evaluation has been completely banned by research ethics boards
Because LLM judges require no prompt design or bias mitigation at all
questions.explain: The dramatic speed and cost advantage of an LLM judge call over a human annotation is what makes constant re-evaluation across many checkpoints and experiments practical.

questions.q: What is position bias in LLM-as-judge evaluation, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: Position bias refers to where the GPU physically sits in the data center; it has no mitigation
Position bias is the tendency to favor whichever response is shown first, mitigated by running the comparison twice with responses swapped and only counting a win if it holds both ways
Position bias means the judge always prefers the second response shown
Position bias can only be fixed by using a human annotator instead
questions.explain: Position bias is the tendency to favor the first-shown response regardless of quality; swapping the order and requiring a consistent win in both orderings is the standard mitigation.

questions.q: What is verbosity bias, and what are two ways the lesson describes mitigating it?
options: Verbosity bias is a tendency to prefer shorter responses, mitigated by always picking the longest response automatically
Verbosity bias is a tendency to rate longer responses as better regardless of added value, mitigated by explicit prompt instructions against favoring length and by using length-controlled win rates
Verbosity bias only affects human annotators, never LLM judges
Verbosity bias cannot be mitigated by any known method
questions.explain: Verbosity bias causes judges to favor longer responses even without added value; the lesson describes two mitigations -- explicit anti-length prompt instructions and statistically length-controlled win rates.

questions.q: What problem does a panel-of-judges approach address compared to using a single LLM judge?
options: It eliminates the need for any prompt design

A single judge model inherits its own idiosyncratic preferences (such as favoring its own writing style); aggregating verdicts from multiple different judge models reduces the influence of any one model's bias
Panel-of-judges makes evaluation instantaneous with zero additional cost
It guarantees 100% agreement with human preferences
questions.explain: A single judge model's idiosyncratic biases get diluted when verdicts from multiple different models are aggregated, though this comes at the cost of running more judge calls per comparison.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend periodically calibrating an LLM judge against real human preference labels?
options: Because LLM judges never need any validation once set up
Because an LLM judge that quietly drifts out of alignment with actual human preferences over time produces a confident, cheap, and wrong signal without any warning
Because human preference labels are required by law for all AI evaluations
Because calibration makes the judge model faster to run
questions.explain: Without periodic validation against real human judgments, an LLM judge could silently drift away from actual human preferences while still producing seemingly confident verdicts -- a risk the lesson flags explicitly.
